model_answer: Start with the job and its limits. The agent reads an issue, searches for the code, edits files in the folders its team owns, runs the affected tests, and opens a pull request. The system prompt says what it is for; a rules file the owners control says what it may touch. The harness enforces the hard limits: no write outside the owned folders, no push to the main branch. The tools are narrow: read, search, edit, allow-listed tests, open a pull request. CI grades the change, and the harness reruns the named tests from a clean checkout. Every call is traced with its cost. I would ship it shadow first, then canary on one team.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for a coding agent that works in a large monorepo.
rubric: Names the job and the owned-folder limit
Says the harness enforces the limits, not the prompt
Names narrow tools and no general shell
Says CI grades, and the tests are rerun from clean
Names the trace or the cost as what gets watched

model_answer: The agent answers questions from the customer's own order record and the policy summary, then proposes a refund as its own step. The refund limit lives in the harness, not the prompt. A refund needs the customer's confirmation below the agent's limit, and a person above it or on a flagged order. Each refund carries an idempotency key, so a retry cannot pay twice. Customer text is data; it cannot set an amount. After a refund the harness reads the order back and reconciles against the ledger. I would shadow the proposals first, then canary one low-limit order type, watching reversed refunds.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for a customer-support agent that can issue refunds.
rubric: Separates the proposal from the issued refund
Puts the limit in the harness
Names the idempotency key or the retry rule
Says customer text is data and cannot set an amount
Names a check after the refund

model_answer: The lead agent owns the question and the answer. It writes each sub-agent a brief: the claim to check, the sources to read, and the form of the result. Each sub-agent has its own context window, so the full text stays with it, and the lead receives a structured result with quotes and their locations. Sub-agents get read and search only; the lead alone writes. Every claim must point to a quote, and the harness checks the quote against the source text. A sub-agent that times out returns a partial result, and the claims it did not check are marked as unchecked.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for a research agent that runs sub-agents.
rubric: Names the lead's ownership of the answer
Says each sub-agent has its own context
Names the brief and the structured result
Says quotes are checked against the source text
Says partial results are marked as partial

model_answer: The agent reads the alert, the metric over the last hour, the runbook and the open incidents, then decides: close with a reason, page with a summary, or suggest a step. It has read tools and a page tool, and no write access in production. A page-class alert always pages, enforced in the harness. An unknown metric means page, not healthy. Each decision is traced with its reason. A person samples the closed alerts every morning. The metric to watch is the missed incidents, not the number of closes.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for an on-call triage agent.
rubric: Names the read-only tools and the page tool
Says page-class alerts always page, enforced in code
Says an unknown metric means page
Names the morning sample of closes
Names missed incidents as the scored metric

model_answer: The run is defined in one file: the tasks, the graders, the trials, the seeds and the decision rule. The owner writes the rule before the run. Each task starts from a clean environment, and the model cannot see the grader or earlier scores. Harness errors are reported apart and do not count for or against the model. Each code grader is checked against known passes and known false passes; a model grader needs human labels before it counts. The decision uses pass^k where every trial must succeed, with its interval, and the run is budgeted before it starts.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for the eval run before a model launch.
rubric: Says the decision rule is written before the run
Names clean environments and a hidden grader
Separates harness errors from model failures
Checks graders against known cases
Names an interval and a budget

model_answer: The agent reads one thread, drafts a reply, and shows the draft to the person. The send is a separate step the person triggers, and the send tool takes a reviewed draft id, not free text. Standing rules, such as never reply to a contract, are data the harness reads before any send. Email text is untrusted, so an instruction inside a message cannot trigger a send. Outbound network reaches only the mail provider and listed links. The risk I would name first is an email that asks for the inbox to be forwarded, so the harness cuts one leg of that attack: the send.
prompt: Walk me through the harness for a browser agent that handles a person's email.
rubric: Separates the draft from the send
Says the send takes a reviewed draft id
Says email text cannot trigger a send
Names the outbound network limit
Names the injection risk and the leg it cuts

model_answer: First, the stop reason and the last tool result: did the run claim done without a passing run? Then the check's own output, to see what it compared. The done claim is a claim, not proof. I look for the edit the checks should have caught, and for a turn where the agent stopped testing. I want to know whether the checks ran on the final files or on an earlier snapshot. The fix belongs in the harness: refuse done until the named checks pass on the final state.
prompt: This trace ends done and the checks fail: what do you look at first?
rubric: Looks at the stop reason and the done claim first
Reads the check's output to see what it compared
Asks whether the checks ran on the final files
Names the harness fix: refuse done without a passing run

model_answer: No error and an early stop means something ended the loop on purpose or by mistake. I look at the stop reason and the last reply: was it end of turn, or a cut-off inside a tool use? Then the exits: is there a turn limit or a breaker that fired without a log line? The unused budget tells me the budget was not the cause. I check whether a tool result looked final to the loop, and whether the harness logged the decision to stop.
prompt: This trace stops at turn 3 with no error, and half the token budget is unused: what do you look at first?
rubric: Reads the stop reason and the last reply
Checks for a cut-off tool use
Looks for an exit that fired without a log line
Uses the unused budget to rule something out

model_answer: I look at the cost by call, not the total. Which call grew, and in what: input tokens, output tokens, or retries? A jump in input often means context that was resent, or a tool result that stopped being cleared. A jump in calls means a loop that did not stop. I check the model and the effort setting, since a changed setting moves cost too. Then I compare the setup with last week's, to see what changed.
prompt: The same task cost ten times more than last week's run. What do you look at first?
rubric: Breaks the cost down by call
Separates input, output and retries
Names resent context or uncleared results
Checks for a loop that did not stop
Checks what changed in the setup

model_answer: Repeated reads mean the model did not keep what it read, or the read did not return what it needed. I look at the tool results: are they empty, truncated or in the wrong format? Then at context: did an earlier result get cleared before the model needed it? I check whether the file is too large for the window, and whether the prompt tells the model to stop reading. The fix is usually in the harness: return the needed part, and keep the result.
prompt: The model asks for the same file five times in a row. What do you look at first?
rubric: Checks whether the results were empty or truncated
Checks whether an earlier result was cleared early
Considers the file's size against the window
Names a harness fix, not only a prompt fix

model_answer: A passing test says nothing about where data went. First, where the secret came from: a read the permissions allowed, or a file the sandbox should have refused. Then the path into the summary: which call wrote it. I check whether the secret was ever in a tool result, and which permission let that read run. The leak is a permission or sandbox failure, so the fix is a permission rule or a path confinement, with redaction at the write as a backstop; the tests are not the place to catch it.
prompt: The tests pass, but a secret appears in the summary. What do you look at first?
rubric: Says a passing test does not show where data went
Traces the secret's source read
Finds which permission or sandbox allowed the read
Names a permission or confinement fix, not only redaction

model_answer: This is a retry loop without a breaker. I look at the error text: does it say what to do next, or only that it failed? Then the retry policy: is there a maximum number of attempts, and is the wait the same each time? I check whether the error is permanent, such as a missing file, which should not be retried at all. The fix is a breaker that stops after a fixed number of identical failures and hands the task to a person with the attempts.
prompt: The same tool call fails the same way every retry, and the run keeps going. What do you look at first?
rubric: Notes that the error repeats with no change
Checks whether the error text says what to do next
Checks the retry limit and the wait
Asks whether the error is permanent
Names a breaker and a hand-off

model_answer: I built a small evaluation harness for a team's tool-calling agent. It ran a fixed set of tasks and reported a pass rate. What I did not expect was that the agent passed more tasks when the harness was slower, because the timeouts cut off its loops, and the pass rate was measuring the timeouts. I found it by reading transcripts, not the scores. I changed the timeout to count as a failure, and I wrote the decision rule before the next run.
prompt: Tell me about a harness you built. What did it do that you did not expect?
rubric: Names a concrete harness and its purpose
Says what happened that was not expected
Shows how it was found, from transcripts or a trace
Says what changed, with the result
Keeps the story to what the speaker did

model_answer: An agent I ran for a week closed support tickets that were still open. The tickets reopened, and the close rate looked good until someone counted the reopens. I changed the score: a close counts only if the ticket stays closed for seven days. I also added a permission that stopped the agent from closing a ticket with a refund attached, because that was where the errors were. The reopen rate fell, and I report it with the number and the window it came from.
prompt: Tell me about an agent failure you ran or shipped. What did you change afterwards?
rubric: Names the failure plainly
Says how it was noticed
Says what changed in the harness or the score
Gives the measure and its window
Says what the first fix missed, if anything

model_answer: A colleague wanted the agent to have a shell, so it could do any task. I thought a narrow set of tools would be safer and easier to test. We wrote both designs for one task and ran them on the same seeds. The narrow one passed fewer tasks, but its failures were easy to read, and the shell version could delete files outside the task. We chose narrow tools for the first release and added a command allow-list later. I was right about the risk, and he was right that the agent needed to do more.
prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone about an agent's design. How did it end?
rubric: Names the disagreement and both positions
Says how it was tested or decided
Shows what each side got right
Says how it ended, including what was given up

model_answer: We compared two prompts on a set of tasks, with five trials each. The new prompt passed more tasks, but the intervals were wide and overlapped. I said that in the review, and we ran more trials before deciding. With twenty trials the difference held on the same tasks, and I reported the interval and the trial count with the number. I would not have claimed the gain from the first run.

rubric: Names the thing measured and its size
Gives the number with its trials and interval
